title: National Preparedness Month: Tornados
description:
The topic of staying prepared for anything that comes your way is especially relevant because of all the current issues involving inclement weather and natural disasters.
SrA Taylor Neuharth, emergency management technician, is here to give you some tips for staying prepared during a tornado.

“Disasters Don’t Plan Ahead. You Can.”

Air Force District of Washington | #NatlPrep #PlanAhead #Tornados

transcript.text: - Hello, I'm Senior Airman Taylor Neuharth
^with the Joint Base Andrews Emergency Management flight.
^National Preparedness Month continues,
^and this week, we'll be focusing on how you can
stay safe and prepared in the event of a tornado.
First and foremost, you want to have a plan.
I can't stress enough how important it is to have a plan
for not just yourself but your family and pets, too.
If your house doesn't have a basement,
the safest place to seek shelter
is an interior room free of windows and on the ground floor.
Once you have made it into the room, maintain
as low a profile as possible until the tornado has passed.
If you are outside in the event of a tornado,
the safest place to seek shelter is
in a drainage ditch or other low-lying depression
that is below the surface of the ground.
Once you have located a suitable area,
lay facedown and cover the back of your neck
and head until the tornado passes.
After the tornado has passed, make sure the scene is safe
and everyone is accounted for.
Take note of downed power lines or leaking gas lines
and report them as soon as possible
to emergency services and maintenance workers.
As with many disasters, having an emergency preparedness kit
can mean the difference between life and death.
It should contain everything you and your family will need
to survive should there be a mass disruption in utilities.
A general rule of thumb is to have one gallon of water
per person per day, in addition to canned food,
a can opener, a hand-crank radio,
food for your pets, and a first-aid kid.
For more information on how to prepare
for tornadoes, visit ready.gov.
